They abandon both sides and escape together, pursued but no longer willing to let either faction decide their allegiance or their future.

recaps.text: Across branching histories, two rival powers alter events to create futures favorable to themselves. Red is a highly successful operative of the machine-like Agency; Blue works for Garden, whose influence grows through living networks. After completing a violent intervention, Red finds a letter from Blue marked for destruction after reading. The message is both a boast and a challenge. Red answers, and the rivals begin leaving correspondence where only a time-traveling enemy with knowledge of the contested strand could find it. Their early letters trade insults, compare methods, and acknowledge the pleasure each takes in frustrating the other. Every contact is unauthorized and could be treated as treason, yet each agent continues her assignments while watching for the next message from the opponent she has never properly met.

Red and Blue carry out interventions in widely separated eras, sometimes undoing one another's work and sometimes recognizing the other's hand only after a strand has changed. Their letters become more elaborate: one must be read in an unusual natural process, another is concealed in matter or history that can survive for ages. The ingenuity is partly camouflage, but it also becomes a gift each designs for the other. Boasting gives way to curiosity about how each was made, what her faction expects, and what solitude feels like for an agent who is valued chiefly as a weapon. Neither can safely give a straightforward account of herself, yet the correspondence creates a private space outside Agency and Garden. The war continues around them, while defeating the rival increasingly matters less than being understood by her.

The correspondence has become the center of both agents' lives. Red and Blue no longer write merely to display skill; they confess longing, imagine encounters, and study entire strands for traces of one another. Each understands that the other is dangerous and that their loyalties should make intimacy impossible. Even so, admiration becomes love. They take greater risks in choosing hiding places and in lingering near interventions where their paths might cross. The language of winning and losing changes: neither wants a final victory that would erase the other or the histories through which they communicate. Their factions still send them to make incompatible futures, and both Red's Commandant and the collective awareness of Garden demand results. The secret relationship therefore threatens not only their careers but their identities as exemplary agents created by opposing systems.

Signs of surveillance close around the lovers. Garden's Seeker follows disturbances that point toward Blue's unauthorized contact, while the Agency scrutinizes Red's actions and divided attention. Red and Blue try to protect one another through indirection, but every new letter supplies evidence that can be traced across the braid of time. They contemplate a life outside the war even though neither knows whether there is any strand beyond the reach of both powers. Garden gains control of Blue and turns the correspondence into a weapon. A final message is prepared for Red: intimate enough that she will accept it, but carrying an attack designed specifically to destroy her. Blue appears to comply, leaving Red to face a letter whose meaning cannot be separated from the danger inside it.

Red reads and consumes Blue's lethal letter. The poison takes hold, apparently completing Garden's plan and punishing both agents through the trust they created. Yet Blue has built another design underneath the order she was forced to obey. Across their earlier correspondence she left preparations and clues that allow Red to withstand the attack and understand how to find her. Red moves through the accumulated history of their letters, recovers, and refuses the Agency's claim on her. Blue, meanwhile, is held by Garden after carrying out the sentence. Red follows the route their messages have made through time and reaches her. She frees Blue, and the two agents abandon the factions that shaped them. Agency and Garden still contest the strands and will hunt the defectors, but Red and Blue escape together. Their private exchange becomes an open choice: instead of winning the war for either side, they choose a future made with each other.

characters.description: An eighteen-year-old preparing to leave for college after spending the summer organizing her mother's latest wedding. Efficient, stylish, and wary of dependence, Remy treats romance as a temporary arrangement and prefers to end relationships before anyone can hurt her. Her late father's one famous song is the unwelcome basis for other people's belief in lasting love.
characters.name: Remy Starr

characters.description: A cheerful, impulsive musician who becomes immediately interested in Remy. He is untidy, persistent, and comfortable expressing affection, making him a poor match for the orderly, low-risk relationships she usually chooses. He plays in the local band Truth Squad with his close friends.
characters.name: Dexter Jones

characters.description: Remy's mother, a successful romance novelist about to marry for the fifth time. Barbara believes intensely in each new love despite the evidence of her previous divorces. Creative and emotionally hopeful, she depends on Remy's practical help with arrangements and crises.
characters.name: Barbara Starr

characters.description: Remy's older brother, a gentle, absent-minded young man whose emotional openness contrasts with her guardedness. He is devoted to his girlfriend Jennifer Anne and is willing to build a relationship without the rules Remy uses to protect herself.
characters.name: Chris Starr

characters.description: Barbara's newest fiancé, a car dealer entering a family accustomed to husbands coming and going. His approaching marriage creates much of Remy's early workload and gives her another case against which to test her certainty that adult love does not last.
characters.name: Don Davis

characters.description: One of Remy's closest friends, sociable and emotionally direct. Her own troubled relationship makes it harder for Remy to reduce every romantic problem to a clean breakup, and the friends' summer conversations repeatedly test the advice Remy gives so confidently.
characters.name: Lissa

characters.description: A sharp, observant member of Remy's close group of friends. Chloe understands Remy's dating rules and defenses but does not always accept the conclusions Remy draws from them, offering a perspective that is loyal without being uncritical.
characters.name: Chloe

characters.description: Remy's quieter friend, marked by the earlier loss of her parents and less willing than the others to treat emotional attachment casually. Her experience gives the group's discussions of love, risk, and family a perspective Remy's rules cannot fully contain.
characters.name: Jess

characters.description: Chris's affectionate and highly organized girlfriend. Jennifer Anne embraces plans, domestic rituals, and visible commitment with an enthusiasm that Remy finds excessive, though her steady place in Chris's life challenges the family's expectation that relationships inevitably collapse.
characters.name: Jennifer Anne

characters.description: One of Dexter's Truth Squad bandmates and housemates. Lucas is more grounded than Dexter and helps Remy see the loyal, makeshift family surrounding the band beneath its poor organization and uncertain professional prospects.
characters.name: Lucas

characters.description: A member of Truth Squad whose talk, rehearsals, and daily disorder are part of the communal life Dexter introduces to Remy. His friendship with the other musicians shows that their ambitions matter to them even when the band appears chaotic from outside.
characters.name: Ted

recaps.ending: After pushing Dexter away, Remy discovers that the emotional detachment she prized does not protect her from missing him or regretting the hurt she caused. The summer's other relationships also resist her simple rules: her friends make choices she cannot control, Chris and Jennifer Anne demonstrate genuine commitment, and Barbara and Don continue trying to build a marriage instead of treating conflict as automatic proof of failure. Remy finally admits that loving someone cannot be made safe by scheduling the end in advance. She seeks Dexter out and tells him honestly that her feelings are real. Their reconciliation does not offer a guarantee that the relationship will last forever, particularly with Remy preparing to leave for Stanford, but she accepts uncertainty rather than using it as a reason not to love him. Her father's lullaby no longer functions only as evidence of abandonment; Remy can recognize that an imperfect or unfinished love may still matter. She ends the summer willing to carry that change into college and to let Dexter be part of her future without demanding proof of its outcome.
recaps.in_short: Remy Starr manages her successful novelist mother's fifth wedding while preparing to leave for Stanford. Convinced by family history that love always fails, she dates controlled, suitable boys and breaks up before becoming vulnerable. Dexter Jones, an affectionate but disorganized musician, violates all her rules. What begins as an unwanted pursuit becomes Remy's most important relationship as she joins his circle of bandmates and allows him into her carefully ordered life. Her friends' romantic problems, her brother Chris's steady commitment to Jennifer Anne, and Barbara's new marriage reveal that neither cynicism nor optimism can eliminate risk. Frightened by how much Dexter matters, Remy ends the relationship and tries to return to emotional distance, only to find that detachment now feels like loss. Before leaving for college, she reconciles with Dexter and admits she loves him. They cannot promise permanence, but Remy accepts that uncertainty is part of attachment rather than a reason to refuse it.

recaps.text: Remy Starr has just finished high school and plans to leave for Stanford at summer's end. Before she can go, she must oversee the details of her mother Barbara's fifth wedding, this time to car dealer Don Davis. Years of watching Barbara fall in love and divorce have made Remy distrustful of permanence. Her musician father left before she knew him; his main legacy is a sentimental hit called "This Lullaby," which everyone else hears as romantic and Remy associates with abandonment. She applies strict rules to her own dating life, choosing manageable partners and ending relationships cleanly. Her brother Chris and his devoted girlfriend Jennifer Anne seem to follow a different model. During wedding errands Remy meets Dexter Jones, a messy, exuberant musician who declares his interest without fitting any of her requirements. She dismisses him, but his persistence and openness make him difficult to keep within the categories that usually let her stay in control.

Barbara and Don marry, adding another official beginning to the Starr family's history of relationships. Remy's close friends Lissa, Chloe, and Jess provide both support and competing evidence about love: they know her rules, but their own attachments cannot be solved as neatly as she claims. Dexter continues to appear in Remy's life. She meets his Truth Squad bandmates and sees the disorderly house, uncertain gigs, and strong friendships that form his world. His lack of polish embarrasses her, yet his warmth is not an act and his friends depend on one another in ways she respects. Remy begins spending time with him despite insisting that he is not her type. The relationship develops without the careful selection and emotional distance she usually maintains. Dexter takes her seriously while refusing to share her assumption that every romance should be planned around its ending, and Remy discovers that annoyance and attraction are becoming harder to separate.

Remy and Dexter become a couple, drawing her further into Truth Squad's improvised community. Dexter's habits still clash with her need for cleanliness, schedules, and control, but he is attentive and unashamed of caring for her. Their connection becomes less casual than Remy intended. Around them, Lissa's romantic difficulties reveal how limited Remy's standard instruction to leave can be when the person involved still has complicated feelings. Chris and Jennifer Anne's domestic seriousness also challenges Remy's belief that commitment is merely self-deception. Barbara's marriage to Don encounters the adjustments that follow a wedding, forcing mother and daughter to confront the difference between believing in love and doing the ordinary work of sustaining it. Remy continues to interpret every problem as advance notice of a breakup, but she also begins recognizing how often this interpretation protects her from having to risk trust. Dexter's place in her days is no longer easily removable.

As the date of Remy's departure approaches, her relationship with Dexter becomes more emotionally demanding. She can no longer describe him as simply another unsuitable summer boyfriend, because his friends, music, and affection have become part of her life. The prospect of distance intensifies her fear that he will eventually abandon or disappoint her. Rather than wait for an ending she cannot control, she falls back on her old strategy and damages the relationship herself. Dexter is hurt by her determination to treat genuine feeling as a mistake. The breakup does not restore Remy's former confidence. Attempts to resume a detached social life only make clear that she is comparing other possibilities with Dexter and that her rules have not prevented pain. At the same time, changes among her family and friends show that relationships can fail, recover, or take unexpected forms without confirming a single universal theory. Remy must decide whether being right about risk matters more than being honest about love.

Separated from Dexter, Remy finally sees that refusing vulnerability is itself a choice with consequences. Barbara and Don continue facing married life rather than allowing every conflict to repeat the family's established pattern. Chris and Jennifer Anne's commitment, and the less orderly choices made by Remy's friends, demonstrate that no set of rules can predict which bonds will endure. Remy acknowledges that she loves Dexter and that ending the relationship early did not make the feeling temporary or spare either of them. Before leaving for Stanford, she seeks him out and speaks without the calculated distance she once valued. Dexter accepts her return, and they reconcile. Neither can guarantee what college or separation will do to them, but Remy no longer requires certainty before permitting attachment. Her father's song remains tied to a father who left, yet its existence also proves that an imperfect love can leave something meaningful behind. Remy ends the summer prepared to enter college with Dexter in her life and with a more open understanding of love's risks.

characters.description: A bright, privileged, and intensely self-conscious young man raised amid his mother's wealth and adult sophistication. He is observant about his own vanity but rarely free of it, and he enters school convinced that charm and intelligence mark him for an exceptional future.
characters.name: Amory Blaine

characters.description: Amory's wealthy, cultivated, and unconventional mother. She takes him through Europe and oversees an education shaped by charm, art, and social confidence before sending him into more conventional schools. Her influence helps form both his sophistication and his sense that he is meant for an exceptional life.
characters.name: Beatrice Blaine

characters.description: A Catholic clergyman and old friend of Beatrice who becomes Amory's mentor. Intellectually sympathetic and personally affectionate, he takes Amory's spiritual and emotional ambitions seriously and offers him a steadier form of guidance than his fashionable surroundings provide.
characters.name: Thayer Darcy

characters.description: A lively young woman whom Amory courts during his early romantic education. Their attraction is strengthened by their shared confidence and taste for dramatic feeling, but their encounters also expose how quickly Amory's idealized passion can collapse into embarrassment and wounded pride.
characters.name: Isabelle Borgé

characters.description: Amory's Princeton friend and roommate, a thoughtful aspiring writer who is less dazzled by the university's social hierarchy. Their conversations give Amory a candid audience and establish a friendship based on literary interests as well as campus life.
characters.name: Tom D'Invilliers

characters.description: One of the Holiday brothers at Princeton, sociable, irreverent, and attractive to the circle Amory wants to join. Kerry's ease and humor make him an emblem of the glamorous college life Amory admires.
characters.name: Kerry Holiday

characters.description: Kerry's more inward and intellectually restless brother. Burne belongs to Princeton's privileged social world but is less satisfied by easy popularity than many of the students around him.
characters.name: Burne Holiday

characters.description: A poised young married relative of Amory whose beauty is matched by practicality and emotional balance. Amory is drawn to her, but Clara sees through the romantic pose he brings to their friendship and refuses to encourage it.
characters.name: Clara Page

characters.description: Alec's younger sister, celebrated in New York society for her beauty, wit, and force of personality. When Amory meets her after the war, both recognize a similarly proud and romantic temperament, and their rapid intimacy becomes the central attachment of his early adulthood.
characters.name: Rosalind Connage

characters.description: A well-connected Princeton acquaintance in Amory's social circle. He moves easily within the campus world whose approval Amory is trying to win.
characters.name: Alec Connage

characters.description: A wealthy suitor who can offer Rosalind the financial security that Amory cannot. His presence turns the practical cost of her romance with Amory into an immediate choice.
characters.name: Dawson Ryder

characters.description: An intelligent, imaginative young woman Amory meets in Maryland while recovering from his failed New York romance. She is drawn to poetry, solitude, and emotional intensity, and she meets Amory as an equal in creating a heightened story around their attraction.
characters.name: Eleanor Savage

recaps.ending: After Eleanor, Amory's fortunes continue to contract. He protects Alec Connage during a hotel raid by taking responsibility for a compromising situation, accepting damage to his own name rather than expose his friend. He then learns that Monsignor Darcy has died, removing the mentor who understood him most fully, while the loss of family wealth leaves him with little material security. Traveling toward Princeton, Amory argues for socialist ideas with a wealthy motorist, though his political conviction remains part of an identity still forming. He reaches the university grounds and considers the ambitions, poses, friendships, and loves that have fallen away. Rosalind is gone, his college generation has been scattered by war and adulthood, and neither inherited status nor romance can define him. What remains is self-knowledge: incomplete and uncomfortable, but more honest than the exceptional destiny he once assumed was waiting for him.
recaps.in_short: Amory Blaine grows up wealthy, clever, and convinced that he is destined to matter. Guided by his cultured mother Beatrice and the sympathetic Monsignor Darcy, he pursues status at Princeton, where friendships, literary interests, and failed romances expose the vanity beneath his confidence. War breaks up his generation. Returning with reduced prospects, he falls deeply in love with Rosalind Connage, but she chooses a richer husband rather than share Amory's insecurity. His later affair with Eleanor Savage also fails to give him a lasting direction. Amory sacrifices his reputation to protect Alec Connage, loses Darcy to death and much of his inherited security, and experiments with radical politics. Back at Princeton, stripped of the social and romantic identities he once relied on, he ends with no clear future but a more candid understanding of himself.

recaps.text: Amory Blaine is raised largely under the influence of his wealthy and cosmopolitan mother, Beatrice, who treats him as an unusually promising child. Their travel and private habits give him polish and confidence but little stability. When he enters conventional schooling, he discovers that intelligence and charm do not automatically secure the admiration he expects. Beatrice's friend Monsignor Darcy recognizes Amory's mixture of sensitivity, ambition, and vanity and begins a lasting correspondence with him. Darcy becomes the adult whose judgment Amory most values. By the time Amory prepares for Princeton, he has learned how to perform confidence and cultivate an image, but he still depends heavily on other people's recognition.

At Princeton, Amory sets out to enter the university's most desirable social circles. He befriends Tom D'Invilliers and the brothers Kerry and Burne Holiday, joins campus activities, and pays close attention to the hierarchies that determine who is considered successful. College initially seems to promise the identity he wants: popular, cultivated, athletic, and destined for leadership. Yet his academic work suffers, and his fascination with appearances competes with genuine intellectual growth. Tom's literary interests and Burne's independence begin to show him kinds of value that do not fit neatly within Princeton's social system, even as Amory remains deeply invested in that system.

Amory's romance with Isabelle Borgé becomes a test of the idealized way he thinks about love. Their mutual attraction is real, but both are highly conscious of the effect they create, and a trivial awkwardness is enough to turn intimacy into resentment. At Princeton, Amory's confidence continues to erode as academic failure and disappointment close off some of the distinctions he expected to win. Burne Holiday moves toward a serious rejection of campus convention, while Tom and Amory devote more energy to literary work. Amory is also drawn to the composed Clara Page, but she understands that his feeling is entangled with self-dramatization and does not return it. He leaves college less certain of his exceptional future than when he entered.

The United States enters the First World War, and Amory's college world is broken apart. He joins the army and goes overseas, while friends take their own paths into service or separation from the society they knew. Kerry Holiday is killed, and the experiences of the war remain largely outside the detailed narrative, registered through absence and the changed lives that follow. Amory returns to a country moving into a new social mood. Beatrice's death and declining family resources weaken the inherited security that once made his ambitions seem effortless. The transition leaves him alive but without the stable college identity or protected future he had imagined.

In postwar New York, Amory meets Rosalind Connage, Alec's brilliant and sought-after sister. Their shared pride and romantic intensity produce a swift, serious love affair. Amory takes advertising work, but he has little money and no convincing career plan. Rosalind loves him yet fears the strain and loss of freedom that would come with marrying into uncertainty. When the wealthy Dawson Ryder offers a secure alternative, she ends her relationship with Amory and chooses the life he cannot provide. Amory responds with grief and self-neglect, abandoning his job and drinking heavily. The loss destroys his belief that feeling alone can overcome practical circumstances.

Amory's later relationship with Eleanor Savage is intense but temporary, another attempt by two imaginative people to turn attraction into a complete world. After they separate, his social and financial position deteriorates further. During a hotel raid, he shields Alec Connage by taking the blame for a compromising situation, accepting public disgrace to protect his friend. News then arrives that Monsignor Darcy has died, cutting Amory off from his most trusted mentor, and his remaining family fortune is effectively gone. On the road toward Princeton, he debates socialism with a wealthy man who gives him a ride, testing a political language for his dissatisfaction with inherited privilege. Back at the university, he faces the collapse of the roles that once defined him. He has not found a settled vocation or belief, but he can finally recognize himself without relying on the admiration, money, or romance he once treated as proof of identity.

characters.description: A veteran of the First World War who works with Otto Köster and Gottfried Lenz in their small motor-repair business. Robert narrates from the emotional shelter of their friendship, using work and drink to manage memories of the war and the instability of postwar Germany.
characters.name: Robert Lohkamp

characters.description: Robert's former commanding officer and one of his two closest friends. Calm, physically capable, and sparing with words, Otto owns the garage the three men operate and drives their unassuming but exceptionally fast racing car, Karl.
characters.name: Otto Köster

characters.description: The third of the comrades, a sociable former soldier with a romantic manner and a ready store of political and philosophical opinions. Lenz brings wit and warmth to the garage and treats the men's wartime bond as a continuing obligation.
characters.name: Gottfried Lenz

characters.description: A poised young woman whom Robert meets during a drive celebrating his birthday. She has elegance without much money and moves through the men's rougher world with curiosity and tact. Robert is drawn to her reserve as well as to the moments of high spirits beneath it.
characters.name: Patricia Hollmann

characters.description: The young apprentice at the garage. Jupp handles errands and basic work while observing the three veterans whose loyalty gives the struggling business its real structure.
characters.name: Jupp

characters.description: Robert's landlady, an alert observer of the residents in her boarding house. She combines curiosity about their affairs with practical kindness and gives Robert's unsettled life a measure of domestic continuity.
characters.name: Frau Zalewski

characters.description: A painter in Robert's circle whose work and conversation dwell on death, decay, and the masks people use against them. His dark humor makes him a companion suited to veterans who distrust easy optimism.
characters.name: Ferdinand Grau

characters.description: A prosperous publican and acquaintance of the comrades. Alfons values direct loyalty and welcomes the men into his bar, though the increasingly violent politics outside complicate old friendships and public associations.
characters.name: Alfons

characters.description: Pat's physician, who treats her recurring lung illness with a mixture of professional frankness and concern. He becomes an essential source of guidance for Robert when affection cannot alter the medical danger.
characters.name: Doctor Jaffé

characters.description: A fellow veteran who celebrates having survived by spending freely on drink. Valentin's ritual excess reflects both gratitude for being alive and the difficulty of building an ordinary peace after the war.
characters.name: Valentin Hauser

characters.description: An impoverished Russian émigré who works as a taxi driver and moves among Robert's circle of displaced people. His lost social position and present resourcefulness echo the wider instability of their world.
characters.name: Count Orlov

recaps.ending: Pat's lung disease worsens at the mountain sanatorium while Robert remains with her and Otto struggles to keep sending money. Otto ultimately sells Karl, the racing car that embodied the comrades' shared freedom, so that her treatment and Robert's stay can continue. Medical skill can delay but not reverse the illness. Robert tries to preserve ordinary pleasures and to conceal the dwindling possibilities, while Pat increasingly understands her condition. She dies with Robert beside her after asking him to remain close. By then Gottfried Lenz has already been killed in political violence, and Alfons has avenged him by shooting the man responsible. The garage has failed, Karl is gone, Pat is dead, and the surviving comrades have lost nearly every material defense they built against the postwar world. Otto's steadfast aid and Robert's vigil nevertheless continue the loyalty that gave their lives coherence. The novel closes with Robert facing daylight after Pat's death, without consolation or a clear future.
recaps.in_short: In economically battered Germany between the wars, veterans Robert Lohkamp, Otto Köster, and Gottfried Lenz sustain one another through a failing garage, drink, and their shared past. Robert meets Patricia Hollmann and gradually accepts a love that makes him vulnerable to hope. Pat has a serious lung disease, however, and a seaside hemorrhage reveals how little time and security they possess. As Robert and Pat try to live fully between treatments, political extremism grows around them. Lenz is shot and killed during street violence; after Robert and Otto fail to catch the murderer, their acquaintance Alfons kills him. Pat returns to a mountain sanatorium as her illness advances. Money runs out, and Otto sells the comrades' prized racing car Karl to support her care. Robert stays at the sanatorium, unable to stop the decline but refusing to leave Pat alone. She dies beside him, leaving Robert and Otto alive but stripped of Lenz, the garage, Karl, and the future Robert had briefly imagined with her.

recaps.text: In 1928, Robert Lohkamp marks his birthday with Otto Köster and Gottfried Lenz, fellow veterans who have become his chosen family. Their small garage barely survives in an economy where customers and jobs disappear without warning. Otto's battered-looking racing car Karl provides one source of pleasure: its plain exterior hides an engine that can humiliate wealthy motorists. During a drive the men meet Patricia Hollmann, a self-possessed young woman traveling with another party. Pat joins their celebration, and Robert, accustomed to guarding himself with alcohol and irony, is unsettled by his attraction to her. Their first exchanges are uncertain, but she accepts his invitation to meet again. The friendship of the three men remains the stable fact behind Robert's hesitant movement toward a life not entirely governed by the war.

Robert and Pat begin seeing one another in cafés, bars, and on drives, gradually crossing the distance between her cultivated reserve and his rough life among mechanics and veterans. Robert fears that his poverty, drinking, and lack of prospects make intimacy temporary, while Pat avoids giving a complete account of her health and recent past. Otto and Lenz welcome her without threatening the private bond among the comrades. Around them, Robert's landlady and a collection of artists, émigrés, prostitutes, and former soldiers improvise ways to endure reduced circumstances. The garage takes precarious repair work and the men use Karl's speed both for competition and escape. Robert's happiness with Pat grows precisely because neither can assume that money, health, or public order will last.

Robert and Pat's relationship deepens, and she becomes part of the comrades' small circle. They take pleasure in driving Karl and in brief excursions that make the country's economic desperation feel distant. Pat's elegance is revealed as something maintained without wealth; she, too, inhabits a diminished postwar life. Robert begins to imagine continuity with her, though he remains reluctant to name it. The garage's future becomes more uncertain as business contracts and possessions must be valued chiefly by what they can be sold for. Political factions are also becoming more visible and aggressive in the streets. Otto and Lenz respond with the caution of men who have already seen mass loyalties become lethal, while Robert concentrates on Pat and the unfamiliar responsibility of being needed by another person.

During a stay by the sea, Pat suffers a severe pulmonary hemorrhage. The crisis exposes the lung disease she had tried not to let define her relationship with Robert. With help from Doctor Jaffé and the comrades, she survives and returns to treatment, but the danger cannot be treated as a distant possibility any longer. Robert learns the routines and evasions of caring for someone whose condition may improve and then suddenly collapse. He and Pat choose to continue their life together rather than reduce it to waiting for illness. Otto and Lenz provide transport, money, and quiet support. At the same time, the garage continues to weaken and the country's political conflict moves closer to open violence, narrowing both the couple's private future and the comrades' place in public life.

Political violence strikes the comrades directly. Gottfried Lenz is shot during a street confrontation and dies, destroying the balance that Robert, Otto, and Lenz had carried from the war into civilian life. Robert and Otto search for the gunman, driven by grief and the old reflex that an attack on one of them concerns all three. Their acquaintance Alfons eventually finds and kills the responsible man, closing the pursuit without restoring anything. Robert must also contend with Pat's renewed decline. She needs sustained care at a mountain sanatorium, and the reduced garage cannot easily finance it. The two surviving comrades turn their energy toward keeping her alive, even as the business and the possessions associated with their shared independence begin to disappear.

Pat returns to the mountain sanatorium, and Robert stays near her as her lung disease advances beyond recovery. Otto sends what he can and finally sells Karl, sacrificing the racing car that had represented the comrades' skill, freedom, and fellowship so Pat's care can continue. Robert and Pat construct small intervals of ordinary life around medical restrictions, but both increasingly understand that treatment is buying time rather than a cure. Robert conceals fear and exhaustion while refusing to abandon her. Pat dies with him beside her. By the end, Lenz has been lost to political murder, the garage has failed, Karl has been sold, and the future Robert briefly imagined with Pat is gone. Otto and Robert survive, their loyalty intact but with almost everything it once protected stripped away. Robert meets the morning after Pat's death alone and without certainty about what comes next.

characters.description: The first-person narrator, a Londoner with a talent for discovering his own symptoms in medical reference books. He joins George and Harris in prescribing themselves a boating holiday and recounts the expedition, its digressions, and earlier disasters with a mixture of observation and self-justification.
characters.name: J.

characters.description: J.'s friend, who works at a bank and supports the plan for a restorative holiday. He cannot leave work with the others and arranges to join them at Weybridge. George is confident about practical matters and music, though his results regularly fail to support that confidence.
characters.name: George

characters.description: The third man in the proposed holiday party. Harris readily diagnoses himself as overworked and contributes firm views on food, camping, and the division of labor. He tends to direct work from a comfortable position and is capable of becoming lost even when certain he knows the way.
characters.name: William Samuel Harris

characters.description: J.'s fox terrier, whose appearance suggests innocence more than his conduct does. Montmorency is delighted by fights, cats, and opportunities to obstruct a task, and the three men treat his reactions as a fourth vote in their discussions.
characters.name: Montmorency

characters.description: J.'s housekeeper, who wakes the party on the morning they mean to depart. The men have misread the time and initially believe they have been roused in the middle of the night.
characters.name: Mrs Poppets

characters.description: J.'s uncle, remembered for attempting to hang a picture without professional help. The small job occupies the entire household as he loses tools, injures himself, damages the wall, and continues insisting that the task is simple.
characters.name: Uncle Podger

characters.description: A friend who asks J. to take two strong-smelling cheeses from Liverpool to London. The favor makes J. unpopular with fellow railway passengers and creates further trouble when the cheeses reach Tom's household.
characters.name: Tom

characters.description: An attendant at the Hampton Court maze. Harris eventually encounters him after trying to guide a growing group of visitors to the exit; the keeper enters the maze to lead them out and becomes confused as well.
characters.name: The maze keeper

characters.description: An elderly angler at a riverside inn who claims that the enormous trout in a display case is his catch. Several other visitors tell J. and George incompatible stories of catching the same fish.
characters.name: The old fisherman

recaps.ending: Rain settles over the river after the party reaches Oxford and turns the return journey into a cold, dispiriting exercise. The men initially insist that they will complete the holiday, but everything is wet, the scenery is obscured, and another evening under canvas promises no relief. At Pangbourne they finally abandon the plan. They leave the boat to be collected and take the train to London, where a substantial meal in a restaurant restores their spirits. From the comfort of dry clothes and full stomachs, George, Harris, and J. agree that ending early was wise. Montmorency's response shows equal satisfaction. The narrative closes with the dog apparently grateful that the three men have returned from the river alive, ending the expedition with relief rather than arrival at its planned destination.
recaps.in_short: Convinced that they are ill from overwork, J., George, and Harris prescribe themselves a fortnight's boating holiday on the Thames, accompanied by J.'s fox terrier Montmorency. J. and Harris start from Kingston and collect George at Weybridge. Their upstream journey becomes a sequence of mishaps involving packing, camping, cooking, towing, locks, other boats, and their own exaggerated confidence. J. fills the voyage with memories of earlier domestic and boating failures and with reflections on the history of the river. The friends pass Hampton Court, Marlow, Reading, and other towns, create an improvised stew, quarrel with a tin of pineapple, misuse George's banjo, and discover that a celebrated trout is made of plaster. They reach Oxford, but continuous rain ruins the return trip. At Pangbourne they leave the boat and take a train to London, where dinner and dry surroundings convince all four travelers that abandoning the holiday was their best decision.

recaps.text: J., George, and Harris spend an evening comparing their health and conclude that each is seriously overworked. J. has recently consulted a medical book and recognized in himself almost every illness it describes, but his doctor has prescribed ordinary food, sleep, and exercise. The friends decide they need a holiday. A sea voyage is considered and rejected after stories of seasickness, and they choose instead to row and camp along the Thames. They plan a route from Kingston toward Oxford, include J.'s fox terrier Montmorency, reduce their equipment to supposed essentials, and divide the responsibilities with more enthusiasm than precision.

Packing turns into a prolonged contest between the men's confidence and their disorganization, with Montmorency repeatedly interfering. J. and Harris eventually carry the luggage to Waterloo and struggle to identify the correct train before reaching Kingston. George must work that day and will join them later. Once afloat, they move upstream past familiar places that prompt J.'s historical reflections and personal stories. At Hampton Court, Harris recounts entering the maze certain that he could guide other visitors out; his party only grew as more lost people joined it, and even the keeper had difficulty rescuing them. J. and Harris continue toward the meeting with George.

George joins at Weybridge, and the complete party settles into the routines of rowing, steering, towing, camping, and arguing over who has done the most work. They encounter the unwritten rules and mutual irritations of the river, particularly the conflict between small boats and steam launches. J.'s earlier experiences supply examples of tow ropes causing chaos and inexperienced boaters making simple maneuvers dangerous. The men repeatedly condemn in others the same behavior they excuse in themselves. Even so, fair weather, food, and the river make the expedition pleasant between mishaps.

The first night under canvas requires a difficult struggle with the boat's covering before the men can eat and sleep. In the morning, small tasks such as bathing and finding a toothbrush become ordeals. The travelers pass places associated with the history of the Thames, including the country around Runnymede, while J. alternates between serious reflection and stories of the party's incompetence. Harris becomes separated from the others during one episode and gives an elaborate account of fighting swans. Later, the men discover that possessing a sealed tin of pineapple is useless when nobody has packed a tin opener.

Continuing upstream, the friends pass Marlow and other river towns, complain about steam launches, and contribute their own share of inconvenience to traffic. George attempts to learn the banjo, but neither his companions nor the people along the bank welcome the practice. Supper one evening becomes an improvised stew made from the available food, with Montmorency offering a dead water rat that the cooks decline. Further recollections cover the hazards of punting and sailing, activities that J. presents as simple only before describing how easily they go wrong. The crew nevertheless continues toward Oxford.

A steam launch that has been impatient with slower boats is eventually required to tow J.'s party, reversing their position in the river's usual quarrel. Fishing stories then become the chief subject. At an inn, an old man claims to have caught the enormous trout displayed in a glass case; after he leaves, several other men separately take credit for it. George tries to inspect the celebrated fish and knocks the case down. The trout breaks apart and proves to be plaster, exposing all the proud accounts as inventions. The travelers reach the later part of their route as the weather begins to threaten the easy pleasure of the voyage.

The party reaches Oxford and begins the downstream return, but persistent rain transforms the river. Wet clothes, cold meals, and obscured scenery destroy their enthusiasm. They try to maintain the principle that a holiday should be completed as planned, then abandon it at Pangbourne rather than spend another miserable night under canvas. The boat is left to be collected and the men take a train to London. A large restaurant dinner restores their good humor, and they congratulate themselves on the wisdom of retreat. Montmorency is equally content to be home, closing the journey with all four travelers happier about comfort than disappointed by the unfinished route.

characters.description: The first-person narrator and one of three London friends who persuade themselves that overwork has damaged their health. He proposes a boating holiday on the Thames and records the journey, frequently interrupting it with memories of earlier mishaps and reflections on the places they pass.
characters.name: J.

characters.description: J.'s friend, who works at a bank and agrees that the group needs a holiday. Because he must remain at work on the first day, he plans to meet the others farther up the Thames. He approaches camping, cooking, and music with confidence that is not always justified.
characters.name: George

characters.description: The third man in the holiday party. Harris is practical enough to help plan the trip but often avoids work while explaining how it ought to be done. He can become confused by simple tasks and believes his comic singing gives more pleasure than his companions think it does.
characters.name: William Samuel Harris

characters.description: J.'s small fox terrier and the fourth member of the boating party. Montmorency has an energetic interest in fights, noise, and anything that interferes with orderly packing. The men treat him as a companion with strong opinions about their plans.
characters.name: Montmorency

characters.description: J.'s housekeeper, who wakes the men on the morning of their departure after they have misunderstood the time. Her intervention keeps the holiday from beginning even later than it does.
characters.name: Mrs Poppets

characters.description: J.'s uncle, remembered as a man who turned hanging a picture into a household emergency. He insisted on doing every part himself while directing everyone else to fetch tools and clean up the damage.
characters.name: Uncle Podger

characters.description: An elderly man encountered near the end of the journey who claims that an enormous trout displayed in a riverside inn is his own catch. His story proves to be one of several competing accounts attached to the same famous fish.
characters.name: The old fisherman

recaps.ending: Persistent rain changes the holiday from an inconvenience into a thoroughly wet ordeal. The men make one last attempt to continue, but cold food, damp clothes, and the prospect of another night under canvas defeat their determination. They leave the boat to be collected, take a train back to London, and finish the evening with a substantial meal in a restaurant. Warm, dry, and well fed, they agree that abandoning the river was the sensible decision. Montmorency's contented response confirms the verdict. The journey therefore ends before the planned destination, with the friends pleased by their adventure but even more pleased to have returned to ordinary comfort.
recaps.in_short: J., George, Harris, and J.'s dog Montmorency decide that a boating holiday will cure the illnesses the three men imagine they have. They plan to row up the Thames from Kingston, with George joining after work, but packing and departure immediately reveal how poorly their confidence matches their practical skill. On the river they struggle with camping equipment, cooking, towing, weather, and one another, while J. recalls earlier disasters involving boats, household jobs, and travel. They pass historic towns and riverside landmarks, encounter boastful anglers and impatient steam launches, and repeatedly turn minor tasks into confusion. The trip remains enjoyable while the weather is fair, but sustained rain eventually leaves everything wet and the party miserable. They abandon the boat, return to London by train, and celebrate their retreat with a large dinner, Montmorency plainly approving the decision.

recaps.text: J., George, and Harris compare their many supposed illnesses and conclude that they are suffering from overwork. They decide that a holiday together is the cure. After rejecting a sea voyage and discussing the difficulties of sleeping outdoors, they settle on a boating trip up the Thames. J.'s fox terrier Montmorency is included in the party. Their planning already exposes the pattern of the expedition: each man has firm opinions about what the others should do, and all three underestimate the work involved.

The friends reduce an impractical packing list, then make a disorderly job of putting their supplies together. Montmorency contributes by getting in the way. On departure day J. and Harris travel to Kingston with the luggage while George remains at his bank job and plans to join them later. Finding the correct train and moving their equipment are harder than expected, but the boat is finally loaded and the holiday begins. Along the way, J. recalls other examples of simple domestic work expanding into chaos, including Uncle Podger's attempt to hang a picture.

J. and Harris make their way along the river, passing places whose histories prompt J. to mix observation with comic memories. Harris recounts becoming lost in the Hampton Court maze while trying to guide other visitors out. George joins the boat as arranged, completing the human crew. The friends camp, cook, row, and tow with uneven success. Encounters with other river users reveal an elaborate etiquette that nobody consistently follows, and the men's certainty about their own competence repeatedly survives evidence to the contrary.

The journey continues through locks and riverside towns. Everyday problems dominate: opening food without the right tool, arranging meals, keeping the boat moving, and deciding whose turn it is to work. The party is annoyed by steam launches when rowing, then discovers how useful one can be when they need a tow. J.'s recollections of previous boating expeditions add further examples of fouled ropes, misguided towing, and confident beginners losing control. Despite their complaints, the friends continue upstream and enjoy the river when conditions cooperate.

Near the later stages of the trip, stories about fishing become another test of credibility. At an inn, several men independently claim to have caught the same enormous trout displayed in a glass case. When George accidentally breaks the case, the celebrated fish proves not to be a preserved catch at all. Meanwhile the weather worsens. Rain soaks the boat, their clothing, and their enthusiasm, and the prospect of continuing to live under wet canvas becomes increasingly unattractive.

The men try to persist through the rain but finally admit that the holiday has ceased to be enjoyable. Rather than complete the intended route, they arrange for the boat to be collected and take the train back to London. There they exchange damp discomfort for warmth and a generous restaurant meal. From the safety of dry clothes, they congratulate themselves on making the right choice. Montmorency also appears relieved, and the unfinished river journey closes as a successful retreat to comfort rather than a triumph of endurance.

characters.description: The first-person narrator and organizer of the expedition. Convinced that he suffers from nearly every illness he reads about, J. joins his friends in prescribing themselves fresh air and a change of scene. He is observant, digressive, and no more practical than the companions whose mishaps he records.
characters.name: J.

characters.description: J.'s friend, a bank clerk who sleeps heavily and dislikes being woken. He helps plan the Thames holiday and supplies dry comments, strong opinions about food, and his share of the party's confusion.
characters.name: George

characters.description: The third human member of the boating party. Harris is confident about his abilities, especially when singing comic songs or taking charge of a task, though events often undermine that confidence. He has a hearty appetite and a talent for becoming involved in disorder.
characters.name: William Samuel Harris

characters.description: J.'s fox terrier and the fourth traveler. Montmorency treats cats, kettles, and crowded packing cases as invitations to interfere. His small size does not limit his readiness to challenge other animals or complicate the men's work.
characters.name: Montmorency

characters.description: J.'s housekeeper, who wakes him on the morning the trip begins after the travelers have overslept. Her practical presence contrasts with the elaborate preparations and poor timekeeping of the three men.
characters.name: Mrs. Poppets

characters.description: J.'s uncle, remembered in an extended family story as a man who turns hanging a single picture into a household emergency. He directs everyone else, repeatedly loses tools and measurements, damages the wall, and remains pleased with his own usefulness.
characters.name: Uncle Podger

recaps.ending: After reaching Oxford, the travelers start back downriver in worsening weather. Two days of steady rain defeat their attempts to treat the discomfort as part of the adventure. At Pangbourne they leave the boat in a boatman's care and take a train to London, while Montmorency shows unmistakable relief. Warm, dry, and well fed in a restaurant, J., George, and Harris agree that they made the right decision. Harris raises a toast to the three men who escaped the boat, and Montmorency appears to endorse it. The journey therefore ends not with the planned return by water but with a cheerful surrender to ordinary comfort, preserving the trip as a success in their memories despite its many inconveniences.
recaps.in_short: J., George, Harris, and J.'s fox terrier Montmorency seek relief from their imagined ailments by taking a boating holiday on the Thames. They travel from Kingston toward Oxford, repeatedly discovering that packing, camping, cooking, towing, navigating, and simply getting out of one another's way are harder than expected. J.'s account wanders into comic memories and stories about riverside places, while the friends encounter mazes, locks, fishermen, tow ropes, rain, and the consequences of their own confidence. They nevertheless enjoy stretches of scenery, food, and companionship. After reaching Oxford they attempt the return journey, but sustained cold rain finally persuades them to abandon the boat at Pangbourne and go home by train. Dry again over dinner in London, they toast their escape and regard the holiday with satisfaction.

recaps.text: J. and his friends George and Harris compare their poor health, although their symptoms owe much to worry, overwork, and imagination. J. recalls convincing himself that he has almost every disease in a medical reference book. The three decide that a change of scene is needed and settle on a boating trip up the Thames from Kingston toward Oxford, taking J.'s fox terrier Montmorency with them. They plan to camp when the weather is fine and use inns when it is wet. Their effort to make a sensible packing list leads to arguments about what is essential, and J. remembers how his Uncle Podger could turn a simple household job into chaos. The holiday has not begun, but the travelers' mixture of confidence and impracticality is already clear.

The men's preparations become their first ordeal. J. packs and repacks while George and Harris criticize him, then they take over and do no better; Montmorency adds to the confusion by climbing among the objects and attacking the kettle. On departure morning the group oversleeps, struggles to find the correct train, and finally reaches Kingston and launches the boat. As they move upriver, J. mixes admiration for the Thames with historical digressions. At Hampton Court, Harris recounts getting lost while trying to guide a group through the maze. The travelers also begin learning that handling a boat and its towline invites misunderstandings between those on shore and those on the water.

Continuing past busy stretches of river, the party encounters the vanity and rivalry of recreational boating. Harris's belief that he can sing is tested in company, while J. reflects on clothing, manners, and the way anglers enlarge their achievements. A celebrated fish displayed in an inn turns out to have accumulated several supposed captors before an accident exposes it as a plaster model. Towing proves especially unreliable: ropes become tangled, towers lose contact with boats, and people on the bank may not notice the trouble behind them. The friends eventually make camp, where raising the canvas covering becomes another prolonged struggle. A meal and a sheltered night restore their spirits, though comfort requires much more work than their plan suggested.

The journey resumes through places that prompt J. to alternate local history with stories of personal embarrassment. The men contend with an early start, cold water, locks, crowded river traffic, and meals for which the needed tools are missing. A tin of pineapple remains inaccessible despite increasingly desperate attempts to open it. At Marlow they shop for provisions and attract attention as their supplies are carried through town. Montmorency provokes a large gathering of dogs, and George's conspicuous boating clothes do not have the dignified effect he intended. The party makes an improvised Irish stew from the food on hand and enjoys the result. George then introduces a banjo, an instrument whose practice gives considerably less pleasure to everyone around him.

J. surveys the hazards of sailing, punting, sculling, and towing through further examples of novices causing trouble. George's banjo practice continues to meet resistance. Near Reading, the river's pleasant appearance is interrupted when the travelers pass the body of a woman who drowned herself, giving the narrative a rare somber pause. At Streatley, the men decide to wash their clothes in the Thames but succeed mainly in making the river dirty and the laundry worse. Later they meet an angler who gives an impressive account of his catch, continuing the book's running distrust of fishing stories. The group has covered much of the route and remains capable of turning every practical chore into a fresh complication.

The travelers pass through the upper reaches of their route and arrive at Oxford. When they begin the return trip, the weather collapses into persistent cold rain. They try to keep cheerful under the canvas and imagine that conditions will improve, but damp clothes, a cheerless river, and another wet night exhaust their enthusiasm. At Pangbourne they abandon the planned journey, leave the boat to be returned, and take the train to London. Montmorency is as pleased by the retreat as the men. In a warm restaurant, restored by dinner and familiar comforts, J., George, and Harris congratulate themselves on the decision and toast their escape from the boat. The expedition ends early, but companionship and selective memory allow them to count it a happy holiday.

characters.description: The narrator and one of the three friends who decide that their assorted complaints call for a holiday. He is observant, prone to digression, and no more reliable or efficient than his companions, despite often presenting himself as the sensible member of the party.
characters.name: J.

characters.description: A bank clerk and one of J.'s travelling companions. George proposes a boating holiday on the Thames and brings a practical air to the planning, though his fondness for sleep and his talent for avoiding work soon become clear.
characters.name: George

characters.description: J.'s forceful friend and the third man on the proposed river trip. Harris readily agrees that they need rest and helps settle the plan, although his confidence tends to exceed his practical ability.
characters.name: Harris

characters.description: J.'s small fox terrier and the fourth member of the expedition. The men initially discuss him as though he were mild and innocent, but J. quickly explains that the dog is energetic, combative, and eager to involve himself in trouble.
characters.name: Montmorency

characters.description: J.'s uncle, remembered in an extended family story about hanging a picture. He insists on managing every detail himself while sending the household for tools and creating far more work than the modest task requires.
characters.name: Uncle Podger

characters.description: The housekeeper who looks after J. She wakes the travellers on the morning of their departure after they have gone to bed worried that they will oversleep.
characters.name: Mrs. Poppets

characters.description: A boy from J.'s schooldays who works relentlessly and fills his time with improving activities. His example appears in J.'s reflections on the perils of excessive diligence.
characters.name: Stivvings Junior

characters.description: A German singer whom J. and Harris once encountered at a fashionable gathering. Guests who do not understand his serious song laugh because they have been led to expect a comic performance, leaving him angry and humiliated.
characters.name: Herr Slossenn Boschen

recaps.ending: After reaching Oxford, the party begins the return journey in worsening weather. Continuous rain strips the river of its earlier charm, so the men spend a miserable evening in the boat trying to pretend that they are comfortable. George's attempt at music only deepens the gloom. When the next day is equally wet, he suggests leaving the boat at Pangbourne and taking the train to London. J. and Harris briefly object in the name of perseverance, then admit that they want exactly the same thing. Back in London, the three men eat a satisfying supper and go on to the Alhambra. Harris raises a toast to their escape from the boat, and Montmorency gives an approving bark. The holiday ends not with the planned completion of the return voyage, but with the friends contentedly abandoning it for warmth, food, and city life.
recaps.in_short: Convinced that they are overworked and unwell, J., George, and Harris plan a fortnight's boating holiday on the Thames with J.'s fox terrier, Montmorency. They travel upstream from Kingston toward Oxford, repeatedly turning simple jobs such as packing, towing, cooking, opening tins, and putting up canvas into elaborate difficulties. The journey is interspersed with J.'s memories, comic histories, and observations on river life. The friends quarrel with equipment, weather, other boats, musical instruments, and their own uneven willingness to work, but also enjoy old towns and stretches of peaceful countryside. At Oxford the weather breaks. On the return journey, relentless rain defeats their determination, and they leave the boat at Pangbourne for a train to London. Restored by supper and an evening's entertainment, they toast the fact that all three men, and the dog, are safely out of the boat.

recaps.text: J. meets with his friends George and Harris, and all three compare the illnesses they believe they suffer from. J., after consulting a medical reference book, has convinced himself that he displays nearly every disease it describes. A doctor instead prescribes food, exercise, sleep, and less introspection. The friends agree that they are exhausted and need a change. They reject a sea voyage after recalling how unpleasant seasickness can be and accept George's proposal of a boating holiday on the Thames. They plan to travel for a fortnight with J.'s fox terrier, Montmorency. Camping in the open sounds attractive in fine weather, but an imagined night of rain persuades them to compromise by using inns when necessary. They divide responsibilities and produce a long list of supplies. Their planning also prompts J.'s memory of Uncle Podger, whose insistence on hanging a picture himself turned a small household task into chaos. By the end of their preparations, the travellers have already shown that their confidence and their practical competence are not closely matched.

The friends settle the food question, rejecting items likely to leak or spread strong smells. J. packs the clothes while repeatedly losing track of his toothbrush; George and Harris then mishandle the provisions, with Montmorency eagerly getting in their way. After a short night, Mrs. Poppets wakes them and they set out with an alarming quantity of luggage. At Waterloo, railway staff give conflicting advice about the correct train, but the party eventually reaches Kingston and launches the boat. As they move along the river, J. alternates between admiration for the old town and stories about the misleading romance of antiques. He recalls Stivvings Junior, a schoolmate whose constant hard work brought him poor health rather than happiness. J. then becomes so absorbed in the scenery and his reflections that he stops attending to the boat. At Hampton Court, Harris recounts his attempt to guide a group through the famous maze. Confident that he knew the route, he gathered more and more lost visitors behind him and proved unable to lead anyone out until a keeper came to help.

The river grows crowded with Sunday boating parties, prompting observations about clothes and taste. Harris tries to sing a comic song and becomes offended when his companions do not respond as he expects. J. recalls another musical misunderstanding in which fashionable guests laughed through Herr Slossenn Boschen's serious German song because they had been told it was comic. The travellers object to landowners who put up threatening notices to keep people from the riverbanks, though they stop short of acting on Harris's more destructive suggestions. George buys a banjo despite having no experience with it. The party then confronts the difficulties of towing: ropes tangle, towers become distracted, and boats run aground or overtake the people meant to pull them. George is introduced to his share of the towing labour. After several mishaps and stories of equally incompetent boaters, the three men and Montmorency continue upstream.

On their first night under canvas, the men struggle to erect the covering and nearly trap themselves in it. Supper improves their mood, but sleep proves difficult in the cramped boat. In the morning, J. alone makes a show of being willing to bathe until an accidental fall into the cold water tests his resolve. George discovers that he has put on J.'s shirt, while Harris attempts breakfast and makes a mess of the cooking. Passing historic places leads J. into imaginative reflections on the signing of Magna Carta and on Henry VIII's courtship of Anne Boleyn. Later, the travellers search unsuccessfully for an attractive place to stay. Hunger and fatigue make them increasingly desperate before a boy directs them to a house where they receive food and beds. Back on the river, their efforts to make lunch are complicated by the lack of mustard, and a disagreement with three anglers adds to the day's irritation. They sail when the wind allows, continuing past Maidenhead after a stretch in which comfort repeatedly arrives only after plans have gone wrong.

At Marlow, Montmorency confronts a large cat but retreats when the cat calmly stands its ground. The men restock their supplies and leave town with so much food that their departure resembles a procession. On the water they take pleasure in obstructing a steam launch, reversing the frustrations smaller boats usually suffer. Harris briefly disappears while trying to get food from the hamper and later gives an improbable account of struggling with swans. At Sonning, the friends make an improvised stew from the provisions available; Montmorency contributes a dead water-rat, which they decline to add. George's banjo practice receives no encouragement from friends, strangers, or animals. The narrative turns to the hazards of household chores and to memories of learning to row, punt, and sail. Each man claims an affection for work while finding reasons for someone else to perform it. Their recollections of early boating make clear how often confidence placed the friends and everyone near them at risk.

The party passes Reading and reaches the reaches around Streatley and Goring. A washing attempt leaves their clothes dirtier than before. An apparently enormous preserved trout in an inn inspires a succession of local anglers to claim that each of them caught it; when George knocks the case down, the fish breaks apart and proves to be a model. The travellers continue through locks and historic towns, creating a chaotic group photograph when they realize too late that their boat is drifting into the frame. They eventually reach Oxford, where J. reflects on the ramshackle boats sometimes offered for hire, and begin the downstream return. Then the weather changes. Continuous rain confines the men to a damp, cheerless boat, and George's melancholy banjo playing makes the evening worse. When the rain continues the next day, George proposes abandoning the boat at Pangbourne and returning by train. J. and Harris quickly drop their objections. In London, the friends revive over supper and an evening at the Alhambra. Harris toasts their safe escape from the boat, with Montmorency plainly sharing the relief.
